Mahbubey Alam with Gopal Chandra Saha, Advocates-For the Appellant 
Khalilur Rahman with TM Shakil Hasan, and Khalilur Rahman (Helal), Advocates-For the Respondents.

GSH Jamal ----- Defendant-Appellant

Surraiya Jabeen and ors ----- Plaintiff-Respondents
full_judgment:
2. The predecessor of the plaintiff-landlords and the predecessor of the defendant tenant entered into two lease agreements in respect of the suit premises on 12-1-1988 upon creating a monthly tenancy in the suit premises which were, subsequently, renewed from time to time on mutual consent. Lastly, on 22-1-1995 the predecessor of the plaintiff-landlords and the present defendant-appellant- tenant entered into two agreements for monthly tenancy in respect of the same for a period of two years ending on 31-12-1996 at a monthly rent of Taka 12,000 for the building situated therein and Taka 40,000 for the vacant place of the suit premises in total Taka 52,000 to be paid by the first week of every month. In the said agreement it was contemplated that the agreement would expire on 31-12- 1996 determining the landlord tenant relationship and the same will not be extended or renewed any further under any circumstances. It was also contended that the 2nd party tenant would hand over the vacant possession of the suit premises to the landlords on 1-1-1997 without fail upon removing all structures constructed by the tenant therein. It was further agreed by the tenant that in case he fails to handover the vacant possession of the suit premises to the landlords after 31-12-1996 then the tenant would pay Taka 1,000 for each agreement i.e. Taka 2,000 for each day's possession of the same. He further agreed that all the temporary structures constructed in the suit premises will be removed immediately on the expiry of the said agreements. According to one of the clauses of the said agreements the tenant deposited Taka 1,60,000, equivalent to four month's rent for the vacant space in one deed and Taka 48,000, equivalent to four month's rent for the building in another deed as security which would not be adjusted with the rent rather at the time of handing over possession, after the expiry of the tenancy period the entire security money would be refunded to the tenant. The said agreements also contended that at the time of handing over possession of the suit premises the tenant would hand over the receipts of all the paid up utility bills for Electricity, Gas, WASA, Telephone etc. in full which he consumed, to the landlord and thereby handover the possession of the suit premises without any encumbrances. But it is alleged by the plaintiff landlords that the defendant tenant defaulted in paying rent of the suit premises for the month of December 1996 when he paid the same on the 8th of December as such he became a defaulter and is liable to be evicted from the suit premises. It is further alleged that the defendant tenant did not pay the rent for the month of August 2003 till date nor he handover the possession of the same to the plaintiff landlords upon removing the unauthorized structures constructed thereon after the expiry of the tenancy on 31-12-1996 rather inspite of repeated intimations to vacant the suit premises as per agreement he continued to possess the same without paying rent and compensation to the plaintiff landlord. As such the plaintiff landlord, on 2-8-2003, issued a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act by registered post with A/D upon the defendant tenant which has been duly received by the defendant tenant on 6-8-2003. But the defendant tenant did not comply with the requests/directions made in the legal notice. As such the plaintiff landlord filed the present suit on 6-9-2003 for ejectment of the monthly tenant; for payment of the outstanding rent of Taka 49,28,000 for the suit premises from 1-1-1997 till September 2003 at the rate of Taka 2000 per day along with direction upon the defendant tenant to pay the utility costs which may be due and remove the unauthorized constructions made therein, for Khas possession in case the defendant after the decree, does not makeover the possession of the suit premises to the plaintiffs. 

 3. By amending the plaint it has been alleged that the defendant in violation of the terms of the agreement constructed Semi Pucca structures in the vacant Space, Unauthorizedly, and thereby the residential nature of the suit premises has been converted into commercial and, as such, the tenant is liable to be evicted from the suit premises upon removing the unauthorized constructions at his own cost for violation of the terms of agreement as provided in the terms of the said agreement. It is further contended that the tenant obtained order from the House Rent Controller in House Rent Case No. 12 of 1997 to deposit Taka 53,200 per month which is contrary to the agreement dated 22-1-1995 and, as such, the plaintiff preferred an appeal against the said order of the Rent Controller which is pending. It is alleged further that the defendant tenant did not pay the entire amount of rent as per agreement which is Taka 2,000 per day i.e. Taka 60,000 per month in the House Rent Controller. Thus apart from being a defaulter he is also liable to be evicted for violating the terms of agreement as provided under section 18 of the premises Rent Control Act, 1991. It is further alleged that the defendant tenant filed Title Suit No.38 of 1991 subsequently, remembered as TitleSuit No.157 of 1999 in the 3rd Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka against the plaintiff landlords, wherein he prayed for temporary injunction for restraining the landlords from evicting the tenant from the suit premises. Such conduct of the defendant, it is alleged, shows that he does not want to vacant the suit premises rather possessing the same illegally on different pretexts, Hence the suit. 

 4. The defendant tenant contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations of the plaint contending inter alia that since long before, the predecessor of the defendant tenant having good relationship with the predecessor of the plaintiffs entered into two agreements for monthly tenancy of the suit premises on 12-1-1988; The rents were paid regularly. Thereafter the agreement being renewed from time to time after every two years the defendant tenant, is running the business of "Shapla Community Centre" in the suit premises; After the demise of both the original land lord and the original tenant the agreements were entered into and renewed from time to time between the present plaintiffs and the present defendant. For renovation of the community centre the defendant tenant spent Taka 75,00,000 and the tenant having paid rent regularly to the landlord within time he is not a defaulter. Pursuant to the good relationship between the families the tenant did not keep with him all the renewed agreements and the copy of all the rent receipt; after expiry of the lease deeds in question on 31-12-1996 the agreements were renewed pursuant to the discussions between them for the year 1997- 1998 and the defendant tenant, pursuant to such agreement as well as the discussions continued his business of running community centre in the suit premises. But when the landlord did not adjust the rent for the month of December 1995 with the security money, kept in deposit with them, the defendant tenant paid the rent of the said month on 8-12-1996. Subsequently, having failed to get the agreement renewed on requests the defendant tenant a legal notice upon the plaintiff landlords on 26-12-1996 through his Advocate and the plaintiff landlords having received the said notice did not reply to the same, as such another legal notice was issued by the defendant, which returned undelivered. However, the defendant tenant continued paying rent up to December 1996 which the landlord received upon issuing rent receipts. But however, when the defendant tenant wanted to pay rent for the month of January 1997, the plaintiff landlords refused to receive the same with intention to make the defendant tenant a defaulter. Understanding the said intention of the landlords, the tenant, on 8-1-1997 sent Taka 52,000 by Money Order to the plaintiff landlords which the plaintiffs, on 15-1-1997 refused to accept and the said refused having been received on 21-1-1997 by the tenant, House Rent Case No. 12 of 1997 was filed before the House Rent Controller for depositing the rent and since then the tenant had been depositing the rent regularly in accordance with law. The House Rent Controller by his order dated 17-1-2000 allowed the case of the defendant tenant and directed him to deposit Taka 53,200 as rent with the House Rent Controller regularly. It is further contended by the defendant tenant that he was compelled to file Title Suit No. 34 of 1997 (subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No. 157 of 1999 of the 3rd Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka) and obtained an ad interim order of injunction therein which is still pending. Thus the tenant is not a defaulter in the eye of law and he is running his business in the suit premises ad earning his livelihood through the said business. In case the defendant is evicted from the suit premises he will be in grave trouble as such the suit should be dismissed. 

 5. Considering the pleading of both the parties, the learned Joint District Judge framed as many as seven issues including the issue as to whether the defendant having not paid rent is a defaulter, whether the defendant constructed any unauthorized structures and running the business of Shapla Community Center; whether pursuant to the agreement the defendant tenant is liable to pay Taka 2000 as compensation on the expiry of the agreement, whether the tenant is liable to be evicted for violating the terms of the agreement; whether the plaintiff is entitled to get relief as prayed for on evicting the defendant tenant upon removing the unauthorized structures thereon' and recovery of arrear rent including compensation. 

 6. The plaintiffs in support of their claim adduced two witnesses including plaintiff No.3 (a) as PW 1 and the learned Advocate who issued the legal notice as PW 2. On the other hand, the defendant tenant adduced himself only as DW 1. The plaintiff landlords in support of their case made out in the plaint filed four exhibits including two agreements in question dated 22-1-1995 (Exhibit X, XI = 4, 4(ka), the legal notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act (Exhibit 2 series) along with notice of RAJUK and the Works Department addressed top the plaintiff (Exhibit 3 to 3 (gha). On the other hand, the defendant tenant filed three Exhibits namely the judgment of the House Rent Control Case No. 12 of 1997 passed on 17-1-2000 (Exhibit "Ka"), order No.9 dated 9-6-1997 passed by in Title Suit No. 34 of 1997 subsequently re-numbered as Title Suit No. 157 of 1999 showing granting of injunction against the plaintiff landlords (Exhibit "Ka") and the legal notice dated 30-7-2003 issued by Mr Md Nurul Islam, Advocate on behalf of the plaintiff landlords upon the defendant tenant along with the registered receipt with AID (Exhibit "Ga", which has also been marked as Exhibit 2 series). 

 7. Upon considering the pleadings and the evidences on record, both oral and documentary, the learned Jude held that the suit is maintainable, the same is not barred by limitation, the defendant tenant as DW 1 having admitted that the rent for the month of December was paid on 8-12-1996, which is beyond the time fixed in the agreement and the rent for the month of January 1997 having paid on 25-1-1997 and the rent for the month of August 2003 having not at all being paid till date he has become a defaulter. Apart from this, upon examining the payment receipts as appears in the record of House Rent Control case No. 12 of 1997 the Court further held that the defendant tenant did not pay rent for the month of January 1997, February 1998, August 1998, December 1999, February 2001 within the stipulated period of first week of the month, as contemplated in the agreement, as such he has become a defaulter. It is further held that in violation of the terms of the agreements dated 22-1-1995 the defendant tenant constructed unauthorized structures and had been running the business of "Shapla Community Centre"; and the defendant tenant, pursuant to two agreements dated 22-1-1995 is liable to pay Taka 2000 as compensation, for each day's overstay in the suit premises after 31-12-1996; the Court also found that since the defendant tenant violated the terms of the agreement as such he is liable to be evicted. Accordingly the tenant defendant having not vacated the suit premises after the expiry of the agreement, he is liable to be evicted upon removing the unauthorized structures constructed therein with compensation and the plaintiff is entitled to get the arrear rents from the defendant for the period of his stay in the suit premises after 31-12-1996. With all these findings the learned Judge decreed the suit and directed the defendant to vacate the suit premises with 30 days upon removing the unauthorized structures situated thereon and also directed the defendant tenant to pay Taka 2000 per day i.e. Taka 60,000 per month and upon deducting Taka 53,200, which is being deposited with the Rent Controller, every month, from the said amount of Taka 60,000 the Court held that the remaining amount of Taka 6,800 is required to be paid from the date of expiry of the agreement till August 2008 i.e. 140 months which amounts to Taka 9,52,000 as compensation. The Court further deducted the security amount of Taka 2,08,000 from the said amount of Taka 9,52,000 and accordingly directed the defendant tenant to pay Taka 7,44,000 to the plaintiffs land lords. The defendant tenant has further been directed to pay the utility bills for the use of Electricity, WASA, GAS, Sewerage, telephone, etc, from 22-1-1995 till August 2008 and hand over the paid receipts to the plaintiff landlords in default the plaintiff be entitled to get the decree executed through Court. Hence this appeal. 

 8. Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant appellant (tenant) at the very outset admitted that the question for determination in this appeal is whether the appellant is a defaulter as defined under the provision of the Premises Rent Control Act and/or he is entitled to get protection under the said Act. In this respect he submits that after the determination of the tenancy when the tenant remains in possession he becomes a "statutory tenant" as such he cannot be evicted as a default if such tenant continues paying rent regularly within the stipulated time of 15 days of the month following as provided in the statute. Relying on the case of Maria Keshi D' Rozaria vs Hassan Movies Ltd, reported in 41 DLR (AD) 35 submits that the facts of the said case and the facts of the instant case being almost similar the defendant appellant is entitled to get, the benefit of the said decision and, as such, he being a statutory tenant under section 2 (8) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance 1963 which is similar to section 2 (Umma) of the Premises Rent Control Act 1991, he is entitled to get protection of the Act. Thus he submits that since, after the expiry of the agreement on 31-12-1996 the tenant had been paying rent with the Rent Controller within 15th day of the month following, as provided under section 18 (5) of the Act, 1991, the defendant appellant is not a defaulter as such is not liable to be evicted on such ground. He next submits that the learned Judge of the trial Court was wrong in calculating the rent for the scheduled premises, to be paid by the defendant appellant (tenant) after the expiry of the agreements, by deducting Taka 53200 (the rent deposited with the Rent Controller) from Taka 60,000 the compensation money @ of Taka 2000 per day, inspite of the fact that the same is admittedly the compensation money for' each day's possession. Thus the direction to pay Taka 7,44,000 upon deducting from the total amount of rent paid to the House Rent Controller and also upon deducting the security money, kept with the landlords is also illegal and liable to be set aside. He submits that the compensation can never be regarded as rent and if the defendant appellant is liable to pay the compensation then the plaintiff can recover the same in accordance with law, if necessary, by filing a separate suit But under no circumstances the compensation can be considered as rent and, as such, the direction in that regard is illegal and liable to be set aside. Lastly, Mr Alam frankly admits that till 31- 12-1996 the agreements were in force and the ten- ant, according to the terms of the said agreement, was liable to pay rent within the "first week" of every month, but it appears, that the rent for the month of December 1996, the last month of the tenant period, was not paid within time as per agreement rather the payment was made out of time by only one day. According to him since the defendant never defaulted in paying rent during the tenancy period and subsequently. as he is depositing the same with the House Rent Controller regularly according to law, the conduct of the defendant appellant is very clear and. as such, he should not be evicted from the suit premises on the ground of default. Rather, relying 011 the decision of Kalu Mondal vs Begum Fazilatun Nessa, reported in 46 DLR (AD) 53 he submits that the defendant's clear conduct should be taken into consideration and the delay of only one day in paying rent only for the last month of the tenancy period should be considered leniently and on enquiry, as contemplated in section 18 as to whether the tenant was entitled to the benefit of protection from ejectment at the instance of the landlord due to non-payment of rent, becomes all the more necessary when the tenant comes with a positive case, supported by evidence, that due to some kind of abnormal situation supervening at the relevant time it was beyond his control to pay rent and, as such, the tenant be allowed to remain in the suit premises. 

 9. On the other hand, Mr Md Khalilur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the respondent-landlords, relying on the age old principle "once a defaulter always a defaulter" which has been approved by all the superior Courts of the sub-continent and by now has become a unique method for evicting a tenant, submits that since the defendant tenant as DW 1 admitted that the rent for the month of December 1996 was not paid within the stipulated period of the first week of the said month, he has become a defaulter in the eye of law and liable to be evicted accordingly. About the contention of Mr Alam as to payment made only a day beyond the time specified in the agreement', MrRahman submits that the same is no basis as the principle is very clear i.e. once the tenant defaults in paying rent, no matter by one day or more, he becomes a defaulter and, as such, becomes liable to be evicted from the suit premises anytime subsequent thereto. Mr Rahman next submits that apart from being a defaulted for the month of December 1996 the defendant appellant in his cross examination further admitted that the rent for the month of January 1997 was sent by money order on 8-1-1997 beyond time though after the expiry of the tenancy agreement which was not renewed or extended any further after 31-12-1996, and, as such, the defendant appellant again became a defaulter for nonpayment of rent for the month of January 1997. In support of his contention he relied on several decisions amongst which the case of Bulbul Begum vs Mohd Sanwar Belal, reported in 8 MLR (AD) 193; Nurul Islam vs Md Ali Hossain Miah being dead his heirs Amir Hossain and others, reported in 50 DLR (AD) 114; Boshir Ahmed, vs Ayub Ali Mollah reported in 19 BLD 537 are notable. Thus once a tenant becomes a defaulter under no circumstances he can get protection under the law from eviction on any ground not even in a case of adjustment of the rent from the security or advance kept with the landlord at the time of commencement of the tenancy, The payment of salami or advance in excess of one month's rent is strictly prohibited under section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Act which is recoverable from the landlords on an application by the tenant to the Rent Controller within six months of marking such deposit/payment. Thus Mr Rahman submits that under no circumstances, the tenant can take a plea of adjustment of rent from the said security money or advance and thereby save him from being a defaulter and evicted. In support of this view Mr Rahman relied in the case of Md Mushtaque Hossain vs Md Shahjahan Miah reported in 10 MLR (AD) 139 = 57 DLR (AD) 60, Mostak Hossain Chowdhury vs Hosne Ara Salam, reported in 8 MLR (AD) 124; Md Jashimuddin vs Mrs Nurjahan Begum reported in 14 BLD 528; Mymensingh Arya Darma Gnan Prodaini Sava vs Rabindra Nayaan Paul reported in 56 DLR 47; 

 10. Mr Khalilur Rahman next contended that even acceptance of rent subsequent to the month of default will not protect the tenant and that will not act as an waiver of claiming the tenant a defaulter: nor acceptance or payment of rent in lump will save the tenant from the mischief of the law making him a defaulter. In reply to Mr Alam's submissions as to the defendant appellant is neither a "tenant by holding over" nor "by sufferance" rather a "tenant under the statute", Mr Rahman submits that the term 'statutory tenant' has been imported from the Transfer of Property Act. Section 116 of the said Act provides as to holding over. According to him the agreement has expired on 31-12-1996 on the basis of its term and admittedly the defendant appellant tenant was in possession of the suit premises after 31-12-1996 and he was depositing rent on the basis of rate fixed by the agreement, in the House Rent Controller and, as such, he is accepting part of the agreement. Again when the defendant appellant retains possession and the respondent landlords having issued notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act and thereby directing the tenant to vacate the suit premises in 2003 the tenant's possession in the suit premises from 1-1-1997 till September 2003, in some respect, can be construed to be "with the assent of the landlords, impliedly not expressly", to such continuance of possession. As such the tenant after 31-12-1996 continued the tenancy by "holding over". Once the tenant posses the suit property by holding over the terms and condition of the agreement automatically comes into operation and the tenant again becomes liable to pay the rent on the basis of the terms of the agreement as fixed by the parties to the agreement. In this respect he relied on the case of Siddik Ali being dead his heirs Afia Rahman, vs Nurun Nessa Khatun , reported in 43 DLR (AD) 3. On these contentions Mr Rahman submits that the appellant again became a defaulter in not paying the rent to the House Rent Controller within the first week of the month concerned. Accordingly, he submits that the trial Courtrightly held that not only for the month of December 96 and January 1997 but the tenant also became a defaulter for nonpayment of rent of subsequent months of February '98, August, 98, December 99, February' 2001 and, as such, he is liable to be evicted from the suit premises. Apart from these Mr Rahman specifically submits that after receiving the notice dated 30-7-2003 under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act, on 6-8-2003 the rent for the month of August 2003 has not been paid by the defendant appellant till date thus there has been no illegality in holding that the tenant is a habitual defaulter and, as such; cannot get any protection under section 18(5) of the Premises Rent Control Act 1991 and is liable to be evicted from the suit premises. 

 11. In addition Mr Rahman, upon drawing our attention to section 18 of the Premises Rent Control Act, submits that even then the tenant violates any of the terms of the agreement he is liable to be evicted even if he is not a defaulter. In this respect he submits that the defendant appellant in his evidence admitted that in violation of the agreements he constructed Semi Pucca structures unauthorizedly and without permission from the landlords and he did not pay the utility charges, e.g. WASA, Telephone, Gas in accordance with the terms of the agreements and did not return the copy of the bills to the landlords. Thus he having violated the terms of the agreement and having not fully paid the rent with the House Rent Controller the defendant appellant has become a defaulter and, as such, he is a tenant ejectable at the instance of the plaintiff landlords. 

 12. Heard the learned Advocates of both the parties and perused the record. From the facts and circumstances stated hereinabove and the submissions of the learned Advocates it appears that admittedly the appellant, since his predecessor's time was a tenant under the predecessor of the respondent. Subsequently, the tenancy agreements were executed afresh between them on 22-1-1995 under agreement that the tenancy period would expire on 31-12-1996 and under no circumstances the period would be extended any further. It was also agreed that the tenant will vacate the premises immediately after 31-12-1996. In case the tenant fails to vacate the same he shall pay Taka 2,000 to the landlord, as compensation for each days of overstay till vacating. Further the parties agreed to pay rent of Taka 52,000 within the first week of every month. Under such circumstances we find that the matter in controversy in this suit/appeal is very simple i.e. whether the defendant appellant, being a tenant under the plaintiff respondents, is a defaulter by any means at any time during the subsistence of the tenancy agreement or subsequent thereto and whether he is entitled to got protection under section 18(5) of the Premises Rent Control Act and whether he violated the terms of the agreements and, as such, liable to be evicted? However to answer the question raised section 18( I) and 18(5) of the Premises Rent Control Act are required to be looked into in this respect. 

 13. Upon reading the aforesaid provisions of law it is clear that the provisions are equally safe- guarding the interest of both landlord and the tenant meaning the landlord cannot evict the tenant if the tenant performs his part of duties as incorporated in the agreement including paying the entire rent within the time as specified in the agreement and comply with the other terms of the same as specified therein. In the instant case since a specific date has been fixed, mutually, by the parties in the following manner : “প্রতি মাসে অগ্রিম ভাড়া চলতি মাসের প্রথম সপ্তাহের মধ্যে দ্বিতীয় পক্ষ প্রথম পক্ষকে প্রদান করবেন।” the tenant is to pay the rent accordingly and the time fixed in the law (section 18(5) (Ka)) does not require to be called into and in case the tenant fails to pay accordingly, he becomes a defaulter. It is the specific case of the plaintiff landlords that the defendant tenant did not pay rent for the month of December within time which from the written statement as well as from the cross examination, appears to have been admitted. In his cross examination, the defendant tenant, as DW 1, admitted that ‘১৯৯৬ ইং সালের ডিসেম্বর মাসের ৮ তারিখের মধ্যে দেই।’ So from his own admission it is found that the tenant admitted that although the time specified in the agreement for payment of rent was first week of that month but he did not pay rent for the month of December within that time. The tenant whose default has been established by his own admission, he is not entitled to get any statutory protection against eviction. This view finds support in the case of Binning and Co vs Nasirabad Properties Ltd (40 DLR (AD) 89). The duty is always upon the tenant to take care that he does not become a defaulter. Thus the finding of the trial Court as to payment of rent for the month of Deember'96 is beyond the stipulated period of the agreements for which the tenant cannot avoid the mischief of law and since he is admittedly a defaulter in paying rent, at least for one month during the tenancy period he, under the statute, is nor entitled to get protection of law as provided under section 18(5)(ka) of the Premises Rent Control Act 1991' is found to be in accordance with law. 

 14. Relying upon the case of Kalu Mondol (46 DLR (AD) 53) Mr Alam tried to make out a case that the delay of only one day in respect of payment of rent for the last month of the tenancy period should be taken into consideration with a lenient view and the tenant should get the benefit of abnormal circumstances prevailing then, which was, beyond his control for which the rent for that month could not be paid in time. We have gone through the said decision and we find that the facts and circumstances of both the cases are quite different. In the case referred above the tenant could not pay the rent within time because of the situation prevailing then due to war of liberation which was beyond the control of the tenant and the Court having taken a lenient view of the prevailing situation that 'the condition like war of liberation is beyond the control of the tenant', as an 'exception' to the statute for which the tenant should not be found to be a defaulter in not paying rent within time. But the situation in the case in hand is quite different. There is no such material on record to prove that the situation in the present case falls within the purview of 'exception' as determined in the Kalu MandaI's case referred by Mr Alam. Thus similar view cannot be taken in the present case. As such the submission of Mr Alam is not all sustainable. 

 15. It is enough, for the purpose of this case, but since some other questions, such as whether the tenancy after the expiry of the agreements is a tenancy by "holding over" or "by sufferance" or a "statutory tenancy", whether Taka 2000 to be paid for each day's possession after the expiry of tenancy period on 31-12-1996 can be adjusted with the rent and/or whether security can be adjusted with the rent and/or whether the unpaid utility bills can be claimed as rent and whether for violation of the terms and conditions of the agreement the tenant is liable to be evicted from the suit property under section 18 of the Act have been raised, we need to look into the said questions. There are series of decisions wherein all these questions have been answered. In the case of Continental Corporation (Pvt) Limited vs Al-Haj Md Ismail, reported in 16 BLD (AD) 285 = 48 DLR (AD) 90 it has been held that the unpaid utility bills cannot be construed as part of the rent rather the landlord could complain of such breach of agreement if such bills were not paid but nonpayment or non depositing the WASA charges along with the rent would not make him a defaulter for nonpayment of rent or non making a valid deposit. It has further been held by the apex Court that 'the WASA charges was not part of rent and deposit made as in the instant case was not a complete or valid deposit. In this respect the landlord may have alternative way of recovering the same'. Similar is the case in this appeal as to nonpayment of utility bills. 

 16. Next comes the question as to whether the payment of Taka 1000 in such deed (i.e. Taka 2,000 for the entire suit premises) for each day's possession, after the expiry of the agreement can be treated as rent and accordingly whether the trial Court was justified in calculating and directing the defendant tenant to pay Taka 7,44,000, upon deducting the amount deposited with the House Rent Controller and also from the security money, for 140 months after the expiry of the agreement. In this respect the relevant portion, as to payment and security deposit in clause 8 and clause 3 and 4 respectively, of the agreement dated 22-1-1995 are required to be looked into. Clause 8 runs as follows: 

 18. From the above it is clear that the learned Judge rightly held that this payment of Taka 2000 per day is in addition to the rent and since there is no determination of rent between the parties under section 14 of the Premises Rent Control Act after the expiry of the agreement, the settled principle of law is the agreed rent which was being paid by the defendant tenant to the landlord till the tenancy was terminated the same shall prevail in the absence of any further determination and that shall be the rent for the purpose of section 18 and 19 of the Act. Thus the calculation and finding of the trial Court as to payment of Taka 9,52,000 on the basis of Taka 6,800 per month for 140 months upon deducting Taka 53,200 from Taka 60,000 and further deducting Taka 2,08,000, the security money, from Taka 9,52,000 and thereby the direction to pay Taka 7,44,000 as arrear rent up to August 2008 is not in accordance with law and thus the same is liable to be set aside. The landlord respondent is liable to get the arrear rent from the tenant (defendant appellant) But for recovery of the compensation at the rate of Taka 2,000 per day in addition to the rent for overstaying in the suit premises after the expiry of the tenancy is the matter to be sorted out by the appropriate prayer in an appropriate case. In the instant case it does not show that the plaintiffs prayed for payment of compensation amount at the rate of Taka 1000 in each deed, for each days over stay. Moreover, reading clause 3 and 4 of the agreements it appears that the deeds specifically spelt out that the security money of Taka 48000 and Taka 1,60,000 (in two deeds) are to be refunded on expiry of the tenancy. Apart from this the law is also very clear on this issue. Session 10 of the Act clearly debars claiming or making any deposit/advance/security more than the amount equivalent to one month's rent and section 14 provides for refund or adjustment of such deposit within six months from the date of making such payment on an application by the tenant. Thus the trial court, although observed the payment of Taka 2000 as "compensation in addition to the rent" but deducting the same from the rent already paid by the tenant with the Rent Controller and further deducting the same from the security money is beyond the principle laid down by the apex Court in the cases reported in 10 MLR (AD) 139, 8 MLR (AD) 124 and 56 DLR 47 referred above, and, as such, the decision in this respect being not proper is liable to be set aside. 

 19. In respect of the question as to whether the tenant is a tenant by 'holding over' or 'by sufferance' or 'a statutory tenant' we hold that as the defendant/appellant had been found to be a defaulter on admission the question of the nature of tenancy as to "holding over" or "sufferance" or statutory tenant" is no required to be discussed or determined in this case though the tenant is possessing the suit premises, after the expiry of the tenancy, with the implied assent of the landlords, and, as such, the terms and conditions of the agreements automatically became operative and having not paid the rents to the Rent Controller admittedly within the first week of every month after the expiry of the agreements on 31-12-1996 he becomes a defaulter. Once the tenant is found to be a defaulter during the tenancy period, it is immaterial to determine whether he has also defaulted on subsequent occasions. The 41 DLRs case, facts of which are not similar to those of the present case, and many other cases have categorically spelt out and set down the principle for determining the nature of such tenancy, depending on the facts and circumstances of each case, and consequences thereof. 

 21. It is alleged in the plaint that the tenant constructed tin-shed structure in the vacant portion of the suit premises for entertainment of guests without prior consent of the plaintiff-respondent landlords and thereby made himself liable to be evicted from the suit premises under sub-section 1 of section 18 of the Premises Rent Control Act 1991. In this respect apart from the undertaking made by the tenant in clause 8 of the agreements as to removal of the structures by 1-1-1997, he, in his cross-examination as DW 1 admitted as follows: 

 22. So, from the above it appears that the tenant appellant admitted that he constructed the tin-shed structures in the vacant space of the suit premises without prior permission or consent of the plaintiff landlords and, as such, he admitted that he. violated the terms of agreements and thus acted contrary to section 108(p) of the Transfer of Property Act which makes him liable to come within the mischief of section 18(1)(Ka) of the Premises Rent Control Act, and binds himself to vacate the suit premises for which he is not entitled to get any protection of law from eviction even if he is not found to be a defaulter in payment of rent. Under such circumstances the tenant cannot avoid eviction under section 18(1)(ka) of the Act 1991 for violating the terms of the agreement. 

 23. Considering the facts and circumstances stated hereinabove and the decisions referred to by the parties and also on the basis of the principle laid down in the case of Md Nasiruddin vs Md Mizanur Rahman, Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1300 of 2006 (BSCD 2008 page 121) "Even the tenant cannot resist h is eviction if he is found defaulter for one month only and the Premises rent Control Act requires that the tenant must pay the monthly rent in terms of section 18 within the prescribed period to get protection from eviction and not other- wise," we are of the view that the defendant appellant tenant has been proved to be a "defaulter" on his own admission, for nonpayment of rent for the month of December 1996 and also guilty of "violating the terms of the lease agreements" admittedly by constructing structures on the vacant apace of the vacant space of the suit premises and, as such, is not entitled to get any protection from eviction under section 18(1) and 18(5) of the Act. In this respect we find substance in the submissions of Mr Rahman. Thus the defendant appellant tenant is liable to be evicted. Accordingly, the findings of the trial court, complained of herein in this appeal, is hereby affirmed. But so far the calculation to pay Taka 7,44,000 by the trial court, we are of the view that since compensation or security cannot be adjusted with the rent, hence the aforesaid direction of payment is wrong and, as such, the same is liable to be set aside. 

 24. For the reasons and discussions made hereinabove the appeal is allowed in part. The defendant tenant is a defaulter and guilty of violating the terms of the agreement as such liable to be evicted from the suit premises. The defendant appellant tenant is accordingly directed to vacate the suit premises within 30 days, upon removing the unauthorized structures situated on the suit premises in default the plaintiff respondent will be at liberty to get the decree executed in accordance with law. But the finding calculation and direction of the Trial Court to pay Taka 7,44,000 to the landlords being not in accordance with law the same is set aside. However, the plaintiff respondent landlords are entitled to withdraw/receive the rents deposited with the House Rent Controller since January 1997 till vacating the suit premises in accordance with law.
